title: A small AI support inbox loop
promise: Triage one kind of ticket, draft a sourced reply, and leave approval to a person.
whatItIs: Auxx describes a support CRM where an agent can read tickets, retrieve relevant customer records and knowledge, draft replies, and update records. A beginner version could handle one narrow ticket type using a small sample inbox and a written procedure, rather than rebuilding the full CRM.
whoPays: Hypothesis: a small online shop or support team with repetitive questions might pay for less routine inbox work. The supplied page does not establish paying customers or demand.
loop: A new test ticket or scheduled run starts the workflow.
The system finds the relevant customer record and approved policy text.
A written procedure routes the ticket to one supported category.
The model drafts a reply using retrieved material and marks uncertain cases.
A person reviews the draft and decides whether to send it.
The workflow records the category and outcome for later review.
evidence: Auxx’s first-party page describes ticket-created and scheduled triggers, procedures written in plain language, an agent that reads tickets and drafts replies, access limits, knowledge retrieval, and record updates. These are maker-described capabilities; the page does not verify customer results.
uncertainty: The page presents product screens and feature claims, not independent usage results. A student prototype would need sample data, a narrow policy set and review before sending; retrieval can miss context, and people must write procedures, handle exceptions and approve sensitive replies. This loop does not establish that the whole business runs autonomously.
first24Hours: Choose one low-risk ticket category and write a five-rule response policy.
Create ten fictional tickets and matching policy snippets in a local table.
Prototype retrieval plus reply drafts, then compare every draft with a human-written expected answer.

ease.reason: A narrow ticket triage prototype can use sample tickets and written procedures; integrations add work.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small support teams may pay to reduce repetitive ticket handling; demand is unproved.

feasibility.reason: A single ticket category, grounded draft, and approval step fit a small two-week experiment; live integrations are extra scope.

autonomy.reason: The page describes ticket-created and scheduled triggers, retrieval, drafts, and record updates; humans define procedures and review sensitive replies.

evidence.reason: First-party page shows product screens and describes workflows, but no independently verified use or outcomes.

Markus here. I have been building a Customer Support CRM for the last 12 months to help my dad's business. He was drowning in support messages (dealing with returns, product questions, sales, etc) and didn’t have a good way to organize and attack them, often forgetting to respond. We tried attio, freshworks, n8n for some automations. I liked n8n a lot but I didn’t want to leave to another app to view messages and customer info. Tried to build bridges via Google Sheets and Airtable and then went deep down the rabbit hole and tried building my own solution. At that time I hadn’t programmed in 10 years. I stopped pretty much when Backbone.js and underscore became popular and went on to work in commercial concrete, building many of the high rises in San Francisco and Downtown Los Angeles (including the one with lots of graffiti on it). The goal of the app is to automate as much of customer support as possible, from triage to drafting responses to keeping track of history. Features include: - Omnichannel Inbox — Handle email, chat, SMS, and social conversations from one unified inbox. - Email integrations — Connect Gmail and Outlook to sync conversations both ways. - Ticketing — Full ticket lifecycle with priorities, statuses, types, and assignment. - AI-suggested replies — Draft answers generated from conversation context. - Workflow builder: No-code drag-and-drop automation for tickets, contacts, and messages (you can create your own apps too) - Knowledge Base - Data import — Bulk import historical contacts and tickets. - Call recordings & transcripts — AI-transcribed and analyzed voice conversations. (Beta) - AI: Kopilot — Conversational AI assistant that answers questions using your customer data. - AI providers — Bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic, or other model keys. The homepage is https://auxx.ai and you can play with a demo here: https://auxx.ai/demo . It's open source. You can find the repo here: https://github.com/Auxx-Ai/auxx-ai .
